e.etymology: From Greek aura, breeze, the name of a minor wind goddess and the source of the English word aura. It is also a short form of Aurelia and Aurora.

assoc.t: aura, the glow or energy field said to surround a person
aura: Gen Z slang for charisma, as in aura points
Aura, digital picture frame brand

e.etymology: The Scottish Gaelic form of Columba, Latin for dove, the name of the 6th-century saint who founded the monastery of Iona. Callum is the more common spelling.
namesakes: Calum Scott (British singer of Dancing on My Own)
Calum Hood (5 Seconds of Summer bassist)

e.etymology: An English surname from a place in Surrey, Old English sid, wide, and eg, island or riverside land; some families took it from Saint-Denis in France. The noble Sidney family made it a first name.
namesakes: Sidney Poitier (first Black winner of the Best Actor Oscar)
Sidney Prescott (heroine of the Scream films)

assoc.t: Sydney, Australia's largest city (same sound)

e.etymology: The Persian and Arabic name of the jasmine flower, from Persian yasamin. English Jasmine comes from the same word by way of French.

assoc.t: Yasmin, prescription birth control pill
Yasmin, one of the Bratz dolls

e.etymology: From Old French Ameline, a pet form of Germanic names built on amal, work, brought to England by the Normans. Despite the look, it is not related to Emily.
A Japanese name from the stem of akiraka, clear or bright, written with many different characters. It is mainly a man's name in Japan; in the US it is given mostly to girls.

assoc.t: Akira, landmark 1988 Japanese animated film and manga

e.etymology: A Persian name from the old Indo-Iranian word arya, noble, the source of the name Iran. It is also used in Albania, and Welsh has an unrelated word arian, silver.

assoc.t: Arian, a follower of Arianism, an early Christian heresy

e.note: Sounds like Aryan, a word tied in the West to Nazi racial ideology.

e.etymology: A variant of Rosaline and Rosalind. Rosalind is Germanic, from hros, horse, and lind, gentle, but was long ago reinterpreted as Spanish rosa linda, pretty rose.
A pet form of Theodore, Greek for gift of God, and of Edward. The teddy bear was named for President Theodore Roosevelt in 1902.

assoc.t: teddy bear, the stuffed toy
Teddy Grahams, bear-shaped snack crackers
teddy, a one-piece lingerie garment

e.etymology: A spelling of Natalie, the French form of the Late Latin Natalia, from natalis dies, birthday, meaning Christmas Day. This spelling is common among Spanish-speaking families.
From Hebrew Ya'el, ibex or mountain goat. In the Book of Judges, Jael is the woman who killed the enemy general Sisera. In the US it is given to boys about as often as girls.
A respelling of Rosalie, the French form of the Latin Rosalia, from rosa, rose. Saint Rosalia is the patron of Palermo.
The surname McCoy, from Gaelic Mac Aodha, son of Aodh, a name meaning fire. Americans know it from the Hatfield-McCoy feud and the phrase the real McCoy. It is normally written McCoy.

assoc.t: the real McCoy: the genuine article
Hatfield-McCoy feud of 1800s Appalachia
Dr. Leonard McCoy, called Bones, of Star Trek

e.etymology: A pet form of Nora and Eleanor, and in Japan a name element and short form of names like Noriko. Kim Kardashian's daughter North West goes by Nori.

assoc.t: nori, the dried seaweed used to wrap sushi
Nori, nickname of Kim Kardashian's daughter North West

e.etymology: A surname from Michel, the medieval English and French form of Michael, Hebrew for who is like God. In some families it comes instead from Middle English muchel, big.
The medieval English form of Clara, from Latin clarus, bright or clear, made famous by Saint Clare of Assisi, the 13th-century follower of Saint Francis. County Clare in Ireland shares the spelling.
namesakes: Saint Clare of Assisi (founder of the Poor Clares)
Clare Boothe Luce (playwright, congresswoman and ambassador)

assoc.t: County Clare, on the west coast of Ireland

e.etymology: An English surname from Merriott in Somerset, Old English for boundary gate. Long a men's name, it has been shared with girls since the 1970s and now goes mostly to them. It sounds like the word merit.
namesakes: Merritt Wever (Emmy-winning actress in Nurse Jackie)

assoc.t: Merritt Parkway, scenic Connecticut highway

e.etymology: The Italian and Spanish form of Aurelius, a Roman family name from Latin aureus, golden. The emperor Marcus Aurelius is its best-known bearer.
A German and Dutch surname from bode, messenger. Americans met it through Olympic skier Bode Miller, who says it BOH-dee, and many now use it as a spelling of Bodie.

assoc.t: Bode Miller, Olympic champion skier

e.etymology: A respelling of Kailani, from Hawaiian kai, sea, and lani, sky or heaven.
From Hebrew Re'uven, traditionally read as behold, a son. Reuben was the firstborn of Jacob's twelve sons and the founder of one of the tribes of Israel.

assoc.t: Reuben sandwich: corned beef, Swiss and sauerkraut on rye

e.etymology: A Roman family name, a diminutive of Marcus, which is probably derived from Mars, the god of war. It was borne by a Roman general who fought Hannibal and by two popes.

assoc.t: Marsellus Wallace, crime boss in Pulp Fiction (same sound)
Marcellus Shale, natural gas formation under Appalachia

e.etymology: An English surname from Old English byrum, at the cow sheds. It became a first name in honor of the Romantic poet Lord Byron.

assoc.t: Lord Byron, English Romantic poet

e.meaning: Jesus (Arabic form); also short for Isabel
e.etymology: For boys, the Arabic name of Jesus in the Qur'an, also used in Turkish. For girls, a short form of Isabel and Isabella, which come from Elizabeth, Hebrew for my God is an oath.
A modern name, either a short form of names like Jovanna and Giovanni or taken from the band Bon Jovi. Jovie, said the same way, is the heroine of the 2003 film Elf.

assoc.t: Bon Jovi, rock band led by Jon Bon Jovi

e.etymology: A spelling of Madeline, the English form of French Madeleine, from Magdalene, woman from Magdala, the title of Mary Magdalene in the New Testament.
A Latinate form of Eleanor, from the Provençal Aliénor, first borne by Eleanor of Aquitaine. Its meaning is uncertain; one old account reads it as the other Aenor, after her mother.
From Arabic karim, generous or noble. Al-Karim, the Generous, is one of the names of God in Islam.

assoc.t: Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, NBA legend (same sound)

e.etymology: An English occupational surname for a fisherman. It joins Hunter, Archer and Sawyer among trade names used as first names.

assoc.t: Fisher-Price, toy brand for babies and toddlers
fisher, a forest weasel of North America

e.etymology: An English and Welsh surname meaning John's son, from John, Hebrew for God is gracious. It is one of the most common surnames in the United States.

assoc.t: jones, jonesing: a strong craving
Indiana Jones, film adventurer played by Harrison Ford
keeping up with the Joneses, the idiom
Dow Jones, stock index and financial publisher

e.etymology: From the surname and ethnic term Dane, a person from Denmark, used like Scott or Norman. The surname is sometimes a variant of Dean, valley.

assoc.t: Great Dane, giant dog breed

e.etymology: A variant of Jade, the green gemstone, with an -a ending, made widely known by actress Jada Pinkett Smith. A man named Jada, Hebrew for he knew, also appears in a biblical genealogy.
namesakes: Jada Pinkett Smith (actress and talk show host)

assoc.t: Jada Pinkett Smith, actress and talk show host
